Michigan has no shortage of places with ghostly reputations, but only a handful can back up their spooky stories with reports of paranormal activity.

The 2026 HauntBound Index, a new national ranking of more than 6,000 supposedly haunted places, examines decades of published accounts rather than simply recycling the same old ghost stories. The list by HauntBound, a Michigan-based website specializing in haunted travel and historical ghost lore, includes historic homes, hotels, cemeteries and other places where visitors have reported seeing things that have no earthly explanation.

Some are open for tours, some offer overnight accommodations, and others are best admired from a safe distance. Whether any of them actually have ghosts is another matter entirely.

According to HauntBound's state-by-state index, Michigan has 191 documented locations associated with paranormal activity.

Here's a look at the top 10, as ranked by HauntBound:

1. Two Way Inn — Detroit

"Colonel Philetus Norris, later Yellowstone's second superintendent, built this structure in 1876 as a general store and stagecoach stop before it became Detroit's oldest running bar. Patrons and staff describe a figure called the Cowboy, identified by his wide-brimmed hat as Norris, moving through the barroom. A Lady in White, said to be one of his daughters, has been reported on the stairs, and cold spots linger in the old jail cells."

2. The Whitney — Detroit

"Detroit lumber baron David Whitney Jr. built this 52-room mansion in 1894 and died there in 1900; decades later part of the house served briefly as a tuberculosis hospice before it reopened as a restaurant in 1986. Staff and guests describe a sobbing woman near the third-floor restroom and shadow figures crossing the former gallery now known as the Ghost Bar. Servers on the lower floors report dishes clanging or sliding in empty dining rooms and the smell of cigar smoke in the parlor."

3. Fort Mackinac — Mackinac Island

"HauntBound identified six distinct published accounts at this military site. Five later publications retell those accounts. Reported phenomena include apparitions and cold spots."

4. Landmark Inn — Marquette

"HauntBound identified six distinct published accounts at this working hotel, across four kinds of published source. Four later publications retell those accounts. Reported phenomena include apparitions and electrical anomalies."

5. Redford Theatre — Detroit

"The Redford Theatre opened in 1928 with a Japanese-inspired design and one of the last original Barton theater organs in the Detroit area; a nonprofit organ society has owned it since 1985. Volunteers and ghost-hunting groups hosting overnight events report a minimum of eight distinct presences, including a woman who appears on the top floor near the dressing rooms, pacing footsteps through the third-floor halls, and unexplained activity in the basement and steam tunnels beneath the building."

6. Historic Fort Wayne — Detroit

"HauntBound identified six distinct published accounts at this military site, across four kinds of published source. One later publication retells those accounts. Reported phenomena include apparitions and disembodied voices."

7. Henderson Castle — Kalamazoo

"HauntBound identified five distinct published accounts at this working hotel, across four kinds of published source. Five later publications retell those accounts. Reported phenomena include a sensed presence and apparitions."

8. Michigan's First State Prison (Armory Arts Village) — Jackson

"HauntBound identified five distinct published accounts at this former prison, across five kinds of published source. Three later publications retell those accounts. Reported phenomena include apparitions and cold spots."

9. Calumet Theatre — Calumet

"HauntBound identified two distinct published accounts at this working theater. Six later publications retell those accounts. Reported phenomena include apparitions and cold spots."

10. Eloise Asylum Westland

"Eloise opened in 1839 as the Wayne County Poorhouse and grew into a self-contained complex that combined a psychiatric hospital with a tuberculosis sanatorium before closing between 1977 and 1986. The Eloise Cemetery holds more than 7,100 unmarked graves. In the surviving Kay Beard Building, now run as a tour and investigation site, visitors report footsteps in empty corridors and the sensation of being touched while walking the long central hallway."

Why Is This List Different?

There are plenty of websites and apps to help people find a good Halloween scare. HauntBound digs into something different, exploring places with reputations for being haunted long before Halloween decorations became a multimillion-dollar industry.

Instead of ranking locations by popularity or how often a ghost story gets repeated, HauntBound examines the number of independently published accounts, how thoroughly the claims have been documented, and how far back the reports go.

The index doesn't attempt to prove ghosts exist. It measures the documentation behind claims that they do.

“We do not attempt to determine whether paranormal phenomena are real, and we never count a source that only establishes a building’s history as evidence of haunting claims,” the site says.

Haunted, But Can You Visit?

The index covers 6,041 locations across all 50 states and Washington, D.C., including 5,718 classified as family-friendly and 1,983 listed as bookable.

Each location includes a family-suitability rating and information about whether visitors can tour the property, book an experience or spend the night. A place may have a terrific ghost story but be privately owned, closed to the public or otherwise off-limits to curious visitors.

HauntBound also identifies each state's oldest documented haunted site, the location with the most published accounts, a recommended haunted overnight stay, and a particularly family-friendly destination.

The rankings are based on research through Sept. 15, and the national index was updated Sept. 29 to remove private homes, operating hospitals and locations with nothing left to visit.
